title: The Mosquito Story Behind Santa Cruz del Islote
question: Why do people live on Santa Cruz del Islote?
message: This video tells curious adults that people crowded onto a tiny island off Colombia's Caribbean coast for a very ordinary reason, rest from the sea and, as locals tell it, no mosquitoes, then built the island bigger with their own hands and stay for the fish, the visitors and their families.
angle: People live on Santa Cruz del Islote because fishermen resting between catches found a bare little island where, as locals tell it, nothing bit them at night, and built it bigger with coral and stone; fishing, tourism and generations of family keep them there, despite drinking water that comes by boat, power from a hybrid solar and diesel plant, and a sea that sometimes walks into their homes.
ghi_chu_khung: Thứ tự khung tập 4 (khác tập 3: mở ở cổng hầm, bàn ở giữa, outro ở hiện trường): mở ở bàn kỷ vật (cảnh 1) → nhảy thẳng lên thuyền, lời hứa ở hồi ức (cảnh 2) → chuyến đi → cắt về bàn đúng một lần ở chương biển dâng (cảnh 13, nghiêm túc, ba lô ướt trên bàn) → chuyến đi (cảnh 14) → outro ở bàn, con dấu đóng TRƯỚC rồi mới nói lý do (bật ra từ hành động đặt ba lô lên hình đảo trong sổ) → đuôi ở kệ. Không tóm ba vế, không 'Would I move there?', không cặp 'It suits / It does not suit'. Trang phục Wob trong chuyến đi: mũ cói + ba lô khổng lồ (cảnh 4 trở đi Wob ôm ba lô trước ngực hoặc để dưới đất, ghi rõ ở y_hinh); ở bàn: không mũ.

scenes.narration: The island is Santa Cruz del Islote, off Colombia's Caribbean coast. From the boat, it looked like someone had parked a neighbourhood on the sea. It covers about as much ground as two soccer fields. Newspapers often call it one of the most densely populated islands in the world. No one agrees on the headcount, though. Around it sit bigger islands, with beaches, trees and room to spare. So why squeeze onto this one? The answer turned out to be very small, and it buzzes. As locals tell it, the first fishermen stayed because the mosquitoes didn't. I came to see if there was room for one more. I'd packed a huge backpack. That was my first mistake.

scenes.chapter: An Island Made Mostly of Houses
scenes.role: chương 1 (khuôn phóng quy mô): từ một ô cửa lùi ra cả đảo; thuyền từ Cartagena, nhà, trường, quảng trường, thánh giá đặt tên đảo, không đường không xe
scenes.narration: The boat from Cartagena takes a couple of hours, more if the sea is rough. I spent them holding the backpack on my lap like a nervous dog. We both got splashed. There's a shorter ride from Tolú, forty-five minutes to an hour by small motorboat, depending on who you ask. I found that out on the way back. Up close, the island does have land under it. Just not much. More than a hundred houses stand shoulder to shoulder. Colombia's twenty eighteen census counted a hundred and twenty. There's a school, a restaurant and a little square. In the square stands a cross, and the cross gave the island its name. There are no cars. A car here would run out of island long before it ran out of fuel. I looked for somewhere to put my bag down. I'm still looking.

scenes.narration: So I walked around the whole island before lunch. I finished before I got hungry. Then I tried a shortcut between a pair of houses. My backpack tried it too. Only one of us made it through. I pulled. The backpack pulled back. The houses didn't move at all. A kid strolled past, looked at me, looked at the backpack, and kept going, with the kind of politeness that hurts. I took it off and carried it in front of me like a sofa. Every corner I turned, the backpack turned it first and hit something. A cat on a windowsill watched the whole thing without blinking. Island rule: bring less. Then bring less again. By lunchtime, the backpack and I weren't speaking.

scenes.narration: So why here, of all the islands? I had a theory. Treasure. A tiny island, a long time ago, somebody must have buried something. I borrowed a plastic spade. The ground was coral and cement. The spade folded like a napkin. I dug with my hands for a while. I found one lost button and a strong sense of shame. Then I asked around about the island's past, and the real story beat treasure easily. About a hundred and fifty years ago, this was a bare little island with nobody living on it. Fishermen working these waters used it to rest and to wait out storms. That explains a stop. It doesn't explain a town.

scenes.narration: The town part comes down to something very small. Night fell, the fishermen settled in, and nothing bit them. The islands next door have mangroves and beaches, and that's where the biting crowd hangs out. Locals say this island had neither, so the mosquitoes stayed over there. Picture a party where everyone's invited except the guest who bites. You'd stay at that party too. So the fishermen stayed. And since the island was small, they made it bigger. They piled up coral, stone and shells, plus whatever the sea washed up, and later they poured cement. Some of the ground under me was built by somebody's great-grandparents. I tried to help. I found a nice flat shell, carried it to the edge and set it down very carefully. The island didn't get noticeably bigger. Fair enough.

scenes.narration: I didn't take the story on trust. That evening I sat on the edge of the island and held one arm out over the water, like bait. Across the channel, I could practically hear the mosquitoes planning dinner. Over here, nothing. I waved the arm a little, to look tastier. Still nothing. I took my hat off, in case the hat was the problem. It wasn't. At midnight I went to bed with the spray in my hand, unopened, like a sword I never got to swing. In the morning I checked my arm. Not a bump. I have never been so offended to be ignored.

scenes.narration: Next, an easy question, I thought. How many people live here? A figure you'll see everywhere is about twelve hundred. A man who'd lived here his whole life told CNN it was closer to nine hundred. Colombia's national census in twenty eighteen counted a little over four hundred. The one before, in two thousand five, counted five hundred and eighty. Estimates vary, to put it gently. Think of a jar of jelly beans at a fair. Everyone guesses, nobody agrees, and the beans keep hopping on and off boats. I bought a clicker counter anyway. It overheated.

scenes.narration: I gave up counting and just watched. Whatever the real number is, the island is full. Doors stand open. Neighbours chat across the lane without raising their voices, because the lane is narrower than my backpack. Kids dart between walls that almost touch. A foundation and the Colombian Navy repainted the fronts of the houses, and nine murals went up, painted with the community. In the evening I sat in the little square, next to the cross, and the whole island seemed to stroll past at least once. Somebody's radio was playing. Somebody's dinner smelled better than mine. I ate my crackers very slowly, to make them last as long as the smell. And my spray was still sealed. I changed my mind. Small might be fine. Small might be great.

scenes.narration: The next day, I kept track of the boats. The earliest leaves before sunrise, full of nets. Fishing and tourism keep a lot of families here going. By some accounts, the tourists are catching up with the fish. The next boat was my problem. I wanted a shower, and there's no fresh water on the island. No river, no spring, just coral and salt. The Colombian Navy has brought drinking water to these islands by boat. A bank even donated a machine that pulls drinking water out of the humid air. It sounds like magic. It's condensation, the same trick as a cold glass sweating on a hot day. Colombia's housing ministry has also looked at solar-powered machines that turn seawater into drinking water. For now, I showered with a cup.

scenes.narration: In the afternoon I went looking for a socket. In twenty twenty-one, Colombia's energy ministry upgraded the island's solar and diesel power system, with a new diesel generator and a tune-up for its batteries. I plugged in my phone. The batteries took it personally. My phone charged a little, and I decided a little was plenty. Later, speedboats bring day visitors from hotels on nearby islands, and tourism matters more every year. Some islanders reportedly work at those hotels. I joined a group of visitors for a lap of the island. We finished before anyone's ice cream had a chance to melt. Then the fishing boats came home, and the whole day folded back into the island. Every hour had a boat in it. Nobody here ended up on this island by accident.

scenes.narration: On my last night I strung a hammock near the edge of the island. I wanted to fall asleep to the sound of the waves. It worked. I fell asleep to the sound of the waves. I woke up to the feel of them. The sea had come up in the night and was standing politely under my hammock, like a guest who turned up early. I pulled my legs in. I pulled my hat in. I pulled in everything I could reach. My backpack, on the floor, didn't have that option. It drifted off down the lane like it had somewhere better to be.

scenes.narration: Back home, I set the backpack on my desk. It's still drying. For the people out there, that night isn't a funny story. The Guardian reported that islanders sometimes wake up to find water in their homes. These islands sit only about two metres above the sea on average. That's roughly six and a half feet. A local report in twenty fourteen, cited by The Guardian, found erosion along about forty-five percent of the archipelago's coastline. One small island nearby has disappeared completely. Global sea levels are expected to rise by up to thirty centimetres by twenty fifty. That's about a foot. Imagine a table standing in a bathtub, with the tap left running. A hammock story is funny once. Living with it, year after year, is something else. I changed my mind back.

scenes.narration: So why not pack up and move somewhere drier? I wondered about that on the boat out, while the island shrank behind me into a handful of roofs on the water. I drew its boat routes in my notebook. One line ran out to the fishing grounds, where the nets go before the sun is up. Another ran next door, to the hotels. A third ran toward the mainland, for school. Young people who want to keep studying past the island's school have to leave. I tried to picture leaving a place where everyone I love fits inside one evening walk. I couldn't make the picture work. The fish are close. So are the visitors. And this is where their families have lived for generations. One more thing, said quietly. There's no room on the island for a cemetery. People are buried on another island. Even that, they've found a way to carry.

scenes.narration: This morning I tried packing the backpack again, to see if it had learned anything. It hadn't. It still smelled like the sea. I laid it on the drawing of the island in my notebook, and it covered every house. NOPE. That stamp is about me, not the island. The people out there built their own ground out of coral, by hand. They keep it going with water that arrives by boat, and a sea that keeps knocking. A home there takes patience, a good boat and very little luggage. I arrived with a mountain of luggage and no boat. Honestly, I'd go back tomorrow for one more evening in that square, carrying a bag the size of a lunchbox. If you travel with one small bag, love the water and don't mind hearing your neighbour's radio, you'd do better than me. Somewhere out there, a mosquito is still very pleased with itself. What would you leave on the dock to fit on that island?

verdict.label: NOPE
verdict.reason: Wob packs far too much for an island this small, and fresh water by boat plus a sea that keeps knocking are real costs; the islanders have strong reasons to stay, Wob's luggage and lack of a boat do not.

claims.quote: It covers about as much ground as two soccer fields.
claims.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote covers roughly one hectare, about the size of two soccer fields.

claims.quote: Newspapers often call it one of the most densely populated islands in the world. No one agrees on the headcount, though.
claims.statement: Media reports often describe Santa Cruz del Islote as one of the most densely populated islands in the world; the claim depends on population estimates that vary widely.

claims.quote: Around it sit bigger islands, with beaches, trees and room to spare.
claims.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote is surrounded by larger islands of the San Bernardo archipelago, such as Múcura and Tintipán, which have beaches and vegetation including mangroves.

claims.quote: As locals tell it, the first fishermen stayed because the mosquitoes didn't.
claims.statement: According to a story told by locals, the fishermen who first settled on Santa Cruz del Islote chose it because it had no mosquitoes.

claims.quote: The boat from Cartagena takes a couple of hours, more if the sea is rough.
claims.statement: The boat ride from Cartagena to Santa Cruz del Islote takes about two hours, longer in rough seas; reported times vary.

claims.quote: There's a shorter ride from Tolú, forty-five minutes to an hour by small motorboat, depending on who you ask.
claims.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote is roughly 45 minutes to an hour by small motorboat (lancha) from Tolú, on Colombia's Caribbean coast; sources differ.

claims.quote: More than a hundred houses stand shoulder to shoulder. Colombia's twenty eighteen census counted a hundred and twenty. There's a school, a restaurant and a little square. In the square stands a cross, and the cross gave the island its name. There are no cars.
claims.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote has more than a hundred houses (Colombia's 2018 census counted 120 dwellings), a school, a restaurant and a small square with a cross that gives the island its name, and no cars.

claims.quote: About a hundred and fifty years ago, this was a bare little island with nobody living on it. Fishermen working these waters used it to rest and to wait out storms.
claims.statement: About 150 years ago Santa Cruz del Islote was a small uninhabited island that fishermen from Cartagena and Tolú used to rest and to shelter from storms.

claims.quote: Night fell, the fishermen settled in, and nothing bit them.
claims.statement: According to a story told by locals, fishermen who spent the night on Santa Cruz del Islote found it had no mosquitoes and decided to settle there.

claims.quote: The islands next door have mangroves and beaches, and that's where the biting crowd hangs out. Locals say this island had neither, so the mosquitoes stayed over there.
claims.statement: Unlike neighbouring islands with mangroves and beaches, Santa Cruz del Islote has neither, and locals attribute its lack of mosquitoes to this.

claims.quote: They piled up coral, stone and shells, plus whatever the sea washed up, and later they poured cement.
claims.statement: Residents expanded Santa Cruz del Islote using coral, stone, shells and debris from the sea, and later cement.

claims.quote: A figure you'll see everywhere is about twelve hundred. A man who'd lived here his whole life told CNN it was closer to nine hundred.
claims.statement: A frequently cited population for Santa Cruz del Islote is about 1,200, while a lifelong resident told CNN it was closer to 900.

claims.quote: Colombia's national census in twenty eighteen counted a little over four hundred.
claims.statement: Colombia's 2018 national census (DANE) counted 432 residents in the population centre of Santa Cruz del Islote.

claims.quote: The one before, in two thousand five, counted five hundred and eighty.
claims.statement: Colombia's 2005 national census (DANE) counted 580 residents in the population centre of Santa Cruz del Islote.

claims.quote: A foundation and the Colombian Navy repainted the fronts of the houses, and nine murals went up, painted with the community.
claims.statement: On Santa Cruz del Islote, the Pintuco Foundation and the Colombian Navy repainted the house facades, and nine murals were created together with the community.

claims.quote: Fishing and tourism keep a lot of families here going. By some accounts, the tourists are catching up with the fish.
claims.statement: Fishing and tourism are the two pillars of the economy of Santa Cruz del Islote; tourism is becoming increasingly important.

claims.quote: there's no fresh water on the island. No river, no spring, just coral and salt. The Colombian Navy has brought drinking water to these islands by boat.
claims.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote has no natural fresh water source, and the Colombian Navy has delivered drinking water by boat to communities in the San Bernardo archipelago including Santa Cruz del Islote.

claims.quote: A bank even donated a machine that pulls drinking water out of the humid air.
claims.statement: Bancolombia donated to Santa Cruz del Islote a machine that produces drinking water from water vapour in the air.

claims.quote: Colombia's housing ministry has also looked at solar-powered machines that turn seawater into drinking water.
claims.statement: Colombia's Ministry of Housing held meetings on a drinking-water project for Santa Cruz del Islote in which solar-powered seawater desalination was considered as a solution.

claims.quote: In twenty twenty-one, Colombia's energy ministry upgraded the island's solar and diesel power system, with a new diesel generator and a tune-up for its batteries.
claims.statement: In 2021 Colombia's Ministry of Mines and Energy upgraded Santa Cruz del Islote's hybrid solar-diesel power system with a new 125 kVA diesel generator and inverter, and serviced its battery bank.

claims.quote: Later, speedboats bring day visitors from hotels on nearby islands, and tourism matters more every year. Some islanders reportedly work at those hotels.
claims.statement: Tourism is increasingly important to Santa Cruz del Islote; visitors arrive by speedboat from hotels on nearby islands such as Múcura, and some islanders are reported to work at those hotels.

claims.quote: The Guardian reported that islanders sometimes wake up to find water in their homes. These islands sit only about two metres above the sea on average. That's roughly six and a half feet.
claims.statement: The Guardian reported that residents of the San Bernardo islands sometimes wake to find their homes flooded, and that the archipelago sits on average about 2 metres (about 6.5 feet) above sea level.

claims.quote: A local report in twenty fourteen, cited by The Guardian, found erosion along about forty-five percent of the archipelago's coastline. One small island nearby has disappeared completely.
claims.statement: A 2014 local government report, cited by The Guardian, found erosion affecting about 45% of the San Bernardo archipelago's coastlines; the small nearby island of Maravilla has since disappeared.

claims.quote: Global sea levels are expected to rise by up to thirty centimetres by twenty fifty. That's about a foot.
claims.statement: Global sea levels are expected to rise by up to about 30 cm (about one foot) by 2050.

claims.quote: Young people who want to keep studying past the island's school have to leave.
claims.statement: Students from Santa Cruz del Islote who want to continue beyond the island's school must leave the island.

claims.quote: The fish are close. So are the visitors. And this is where their families have lived for generations.
claims.statement: Residents of Santa Cruz del Islote stay close to their fishing grounds, earn growing income from tourism, and belong to families that have lived on the island since it was settled roughly 150 years ago.

claims.quote: There's no room on the island for a cemetery. People are buried on another island.
claims.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote has no space for a cemetery, so the dead are buried on another island.

claims.quote: The people out there built their own ground out of coral, by hand. They keep it going with water that arrives by boat, and a sea that keeps knocking.
claims.statement: Residents of Santa Cruz del Islote enlarged their island by hand with coral and other materials, rely on drinking water delivered by boat, and face flooding and erosion from the sea.
